title: Si vs Sí: If, Yes and Himself in Spanish
seo_title: Si vs Sí: If, Yes and Himself in Spanish
meta_description: Si vs sí: si means if, sí means yes and also oneself after prepositions. Plus sí que for emphasis, conditional sentences, common mistakes and a quick quiz.
excerpt: One accent mark separates “if” from “yes”. Here’s when to write it.

body_html:
Si vs sí is a tiny difference on the page with a big difference in meaning. Si without an accent means “if”: Si llueve, me quedo en casa. Sí with an accent means “yes”: Sí, claro. Sí also means “oneself” after a preposition, and it adds emphasis in phrases like Ahora sí. In speech, the two sound almost the same, so this is mostly a writing issue, and a very common one.

Quick answer
  • Si = if, whether: No sé si viene.
  • Sí = yes: —¿Vienes? —Sí.
  • Sí = emphasis: Eso sí que no. / Ahora sí.
  • Sí = himself, herself, itself (after prepositions): Habla de sí misma.
{{toc}}

Si vs sí: the core rule

FormMeaningExample
siif (conditional)Si tienes tiempo, llámame. If you have time, call me.
siwhether (indirect question)Pregúntale si quiere venir. Ask her whether she wants to come.
síyesSí, quiero. Yes, I do.
síemphasisElla sí sabe cocinar. She really can cook.
síreflexive pronounLo quiere para sí. He wants it for himself.

This accent is a tilde diacrítica, used only to tell apart two words that are otherwise spelled the same. The RAE’s Diccionario panhispánico de dudas lists both forms with their uses.

Si: if and whether

Conditional sentences

  • Si estudias, aprobarás. If you study, you’ll pass.
  • Si tuviera dinero, viajaría. If I had money, I’d travel.
  • Si hubieras venido, te habría gustado. If you had come, you’d have liked it.

Remember: never use the present subjunctive after si. Si tengo tiempo, not Si tenga tiempo. More in {{link:indicative-vs-subjunctive|indicative vs subjunctive}}.

Indirect questions

  • No sé si tengo razón. I don’t know whether I’m right.
  • Me preguntó si estaba bien. She asked me if I was okay.
{{image:2}}

Sí: yes

  • —¿Te gusta? —Sí, mucho.
  • Creo que sí. I think so.
  • ¡Que sí! Yes, I said yes! (insisting)
  • Sí, quiero. I do (at a wedding).

Sí for emphasis

Spanish uses sí to stress that something is true, often in contrast:

  • Yo no puedo, pero él sí. I can’t, but he can.
  • Esta vez sí lo conseguí. This time I really did it.
  • Eso sí que es bonito. Now that’s beautiful.
  • A mí sí me gusta. I do like it. See {{link:tambien-vs-tampoco|también vs tampoco}}.
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Sí as a reflexive pronoun

After prepositions, sí means himself, herself, itself, themselves or yourself (usted):

  • Solo piensa en sí mismo. He only thinks about himself.
  • Volvió en sí. She came round (regained consciousness).
  • De por sí: in itself. El tema ya es difícil de por sí.

With con, it becomes consigo: Lo lleva siempre consigo (She always carries it with her).

Si no vs sino

Another related trap: si no (if not) is two words, while sino (but rather) is one. Si no vienes, me enfado vs No es azul, sino verde. Full explanation in {{link:pero-vs-sino|pero vs sino}}.

Why this is tricky for learners

English “if” and “yes” are completely different words, so learners rarely confuse the meanings. The problem is purely in writing: on a phone keyboard it is easy to skip the accent, and many learners never notice it in the first place. But the confusion can be real: Si, me lo dijo looks like an unfinished “If, he told me…”. Native readers will usually understand from context, yet a missing accent here looks careless in a job application or formal email. Get into the habit of long-pressing the i every time you mean yes.

A quick mental shortcut

Try replacing the word with “yes” or “if” in English. If “yes” fits, or you are stressing that something really is true, write sí. If “if” or “whether” fits, write si. A second check: si almost always introduces a clause with its own verb (si quieres, si llueve), while sí often stands alone or comes at the end (creo que sí, yo sí). When you read Spanish, notice how often sí appears for emphasis in the middle of a sentence; it is one of the most natural ways to sound expressive in Spanish.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Si, claro.Sí, claro.Yes needs the accent
Sí llueve, no salgo.Si llueve, no salgo.If has no accent
Creo que si.Creo que sí.“So” here means yes
Si tenga tiempo, voy.Si tengo tiempo, voy.No present subjunctive after si
Sino vienes…Si no vienes…“If not” is two words
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. Yes, I know. (Sí, lo sé.)
  2. If you want, we can go. (Si quieres, podemos ir.)
  3. I don’t know if it’s true. (No sé si es verdad.)
  4. I think so. (Creo que sí.)
  5. She doesn’t eat meat, but I do. (Ella no come carne, pero yo sí.)

Accents also separate {{link:tu-vs-tu|tu and tú}} and {{link:esta-vs-esta|esta and está}}. All pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

If: si. Yes, emphasis or oneself: sí. One small accent, and your written Spanish becomes clearer and more professional.

faq.q: What is the difference between si and sí?
faq.a: Si (no accent) means if or whether. Sí (with accent) means yes, adds emphasis, or means oneself after a preposition.

faq.q: Does “I think so” use si or sí?
faq.a: Creo que sí, with the accent, because it means yes.

faq.q: Can you use the subjunctive after si?
faq.a: Not the present subjunctive. Use the present indicative (si tengo) or, for hypotheticals, the imperfect subjunctive (si tuviera).
